note: Padding a struct to the cache line size stops two threads' counters from sharing one line.
SoA gives each field its own contiguous stream, so a pass over one field touches nothing else.
A bump allocator never frees individual objects; the whole arena is reclaimed in one shot.
compare_exchange_weak can fail spuriously, which is fine because the loop just retries.
A release store paired with an acquire load is what makes the writes before the store visible after the load.
A volatile sink forces the optimiser to keep the result, so the whole loop cannot be deleted.
A branchless select multiplies by a 0/1 mask instead of jumping, which keeps the pipeline full.
Linear probing needs a tombstone for deletion, or a later lookup can stop searching too early.
emplace_back constructs the element in place from its arguments; push_back needs a temporary first.
An intrusive freelist stores the next pointer inside the freed block itself, so it costs zero extra memory.
Splitting rarely-touched fields into a side table keeps the hot loop's cache lines dense.
restrict tells the compiler two pointers cannot alias, unlocking vectorisation it otherwise cannot risk.
mmap maps the file into the address space directly, so reading never copies through a buffer.
A freelist reuses freed slots via an intrusive next pointer, so steady-state acquire never allocates.
A pmr container's allocator is a runtime property, not a template parameter, so the type stays simple.
reserve pre-pays every growth; a short std::string never touches the heap at all thanks to SBO.
An odd sequence number means a writer is mid-update; the reader retries whenever it sees one.
_mm_loadu_ps tolerates unaligned addresses; _mm_load_ps demands 16-byte alignment or it faults.
_mm_and_ps / _mm_andnot_ps combine a comparison mask with two operands to select without branching.
A power-of-two capacity turns the wraparound modulo into a single AND against a mask.
Slicing with string_view touches no heap; only converting to std::string ever allocates.
